title: Microsoft Three-Layer LLM Routing Architecture for AI Agents on AKS
gist: Microsoft published an AKS reference architecture that splits agent LLM traffic into three separable decisions - semantic model choice (RouteLLM), policy and cost governance (agentgateway), and GPU-aware replica placement (Gateway API Inference Extension over vLLM metrics). The economics hinge on RouteLLM's escalation threshold, whose headline 85% cost saving at ~95% of GPT-4 quality Microsoft explicitly says will not transfer without recalibration, and the whole stack is flagged as version-unstable.

themes.theme: Agentic loops break chat-era serving economics

insights.claim: A single AI agent task can fire hundreds of LLM calls in a plan-act-observe loop, and most of them - tool-argument fills, yes/no gates, summaries - do not need a frontier model.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Inference demand from agents is dominated by cheap calls; frontier-model revenue per agent task may be far lower than raw call volume implies.
insights.locator: The motivation is agentic workloads specifically

insights.claim: Routing every agent call to a top-tier model makes cost and latency scale with loop length, turning agent autonomy into an unbounded spend multiplier.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Cost per completed agent task, not cost per token, is the metric to underwrite when evaluating agent products.
insights.locator: Sending every call to a top-tier model

insights.claim: Round-robin load balancing actively harms GPU inference because it can queue a 200-token completion behind a 100k-token prefill on a busy pod while an idle pod nearby goes unused.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Naive infra choices waste purchased GPU capacity; GPU-aware routing is a real utilization lever, not a micro-optimization.
insights.locator: A simple round-robin load balancer makes this even worse

insights.claim: Microsoft's AKS reference architecture splits agent traffic routing into three separate decisions - which model answers, how the call is governed, and which GPU replica serves it - each handled by a different component behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating AI infra vendors: semantic routing, policy/governance, and placement are three distinct product categories.
insights.locator: Microsoft has released a reference architecture

insights.claim: RouteLLM performs the semantic layer, predicting from the prompt whether a cheaper model matches a stronger model's answer quality using a matrix-factorization router trained on human-preference data.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Preference-data-trained routers are becoming a distinct infra layer; whoever owns preference data owns the routing decision.
insights.locator: RouteLLM checks the prompt and predicts

insights.claim: Agentgateway handles authentication, per-agent rate limits, cost tracking, and guardrails without inspecting prompt meaning, making governance a separate concern from model choice.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Cost attribution and per-agent quotas are becoming table-stakes gateway features - a checklist item for AI platform buyers.
insights.locator: Agentgateway is an open-source proxy

insights.claim: The Gateway API Inference Extension's Endpoint Picker chooses the GPU replica using live vLLM signals - KV-cache occupancy and queue depth - rather than static balancing.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: KV-cache occupancy is emerging as the load signal for inference infra; watch it as the metric serving vendors compete on.
insights.locator: The Gateway API Inference Extension's Endpoint Picker

insights.claim: Agentgateway can call the Endpoint Picker directly over ext-proc, letting the self-hosted path bypass a separate Gateway API gateway entirely and remove one hop from the stack.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Fewer required components lowers adoption friction for the open-source path and weakens the case for a standalone gateway product.
insights.locator: Agentgateway calls the Endpoint Picker directly over ext-proc

themes.theme: The escalation threshold is the load-bearing number

insights.claim: In RouteLLM's own tested pairing the matrix-factorization router reached about 95% of GPT-4's MT-Bench quality while sending only around 26% of calls to GPT-4, saving up to 85% of cost versus routing everything to the strong model.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The headline 85% saving is the number vendors will quote; treat it as a ceiling tied to one model pair, not a portable benchmark.
insights.locator: The load-bearing number in the whole setup

insights.claim: Microsoft explicitly warns the 85% saving does not transfer automatically because it is tied to the model pair RouteLLM was trained on, not to a phi-4-mini/GPT-5.1 pairing, so teams must recalibrate the threshold against their own traffic.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A vendor caveating its own savings claim is a signal that realized AI cost reductions will trail marketing numbers materially.
insights.locator: Microsoft states that this figure

insights.claim: Calibration should be driven by agentgateway's observed strong/weak split rather than by RouteLLM's own estimate, making routing quality an ongoing ops metric rather than a one-time config.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Creates recurring operational work - and a demand pull for observability tooling around routing decisions.
insights.locator: So, the users need to calibrate the threshold

insights.claim: Prompt caching distorts routing economics because cached input tokens are discounted and switching models cools both caches, so the true cost of a strong-model call is lower than list pricing suggests.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Cache economics can invert a routing decision; naive cost models overstate savings from downshifting to weak models.
insights.locator: The post highlights that prompt caching makes token costs tricky

insights.claim: KAITO provisions GPU node pools on demand and runs vLLM, exposing vllm:num_requests_waiting and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc as the metrics the Endpoint Picker consumes for placement.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Concrete integration surface for anyone building GPU-aware routing on Kubernetes; these metric names are the de facto interface.
insights.locator: KAITO provides GPU node pools as needed

insights.claim: The architecture splits traffic between a strong path to Azure OpenAI via an agentgateway AI backend and a weak path to self-hosted KAITO pods, keeping Microsoft in the loop on the expensive calls either way.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Microsoft monetizes both halves of the routing decision - watch whether cost-routing actually reduces Azure OpenAI consumption.
insights.locator: The strong path goes to Azure OpenAI

insights.claim: Microsoft's Foundry model router is a managed equivalent of RouteLLM's semantic layer, but there is no managed option for the Endpoint Picker's GPU-aware placement, which must run in-cluster regardless of gateway choice.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A clear gap in the managed-service map - GPU-aware placement is an unclaimed product slot for cloud vendors or startups.
insights.locator: Microsoft notes that its Foundry model router

insights.claim: The author warns the components are young and field names drift between releases, with the Inference Extension renaming and restructuring CRDs on its way to v1, so manifests should be treated as shape rather than copy-paste config.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Integration churn is a real cost of adopting AI-serving infra now; budget for rework or wait for managed abstractions.
insights.quote: Several pieces here are young, and field names drift between releases
insights.locator: The author warns that the pieces used

insights.claim: The stack was validated end-to-end on AKS in mid-2026 against Inference Extension v1.0.0 and agentgateway v1.3.1, and the author advises pinning versions while treating the decomposition itself as stable.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The architectural decomposition is the durable asset; specific implementations are disposable - invest accordingly.
insights.quote: Treat the manifests as the shape of the solution, pin your versions, and confirm fields against the docs at the end.
insights.locator: The author warns that the pieces used

insights.claim: Adoption can be staged: agentgateway alone for governance over a single hosted model, KAITO plus the Inference Extension when self-hosting one model class, and RouteLLM only once a strong/weak price gap plus abundant easy traffic exists.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Explains the adoption funnel - governance sells first, semantic routing last, which shapes which AI infra vendors monetize soonest.
insights.locator: Teams adopting this can take it in slices

insights.claim: Semantic routing is claimed to pay off for nearly any agent running in a loop, generalizing the cost case well beyond Microsoft's specific stack.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: If true, model-routing becomes a default layer in agent stacks - a structural headwind for uniform frontier-model pricing.
insights.locator: The post suggests this applies to nearly any agent

insights.claim: Azure Managed Prometheus and Grafana scrape both agentgateway routing/cost metrics and vLLM GPU metrics into a single view, making routing decisions and GPU state observable together.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Observability is the connective tissue of AI serving stacks; joint routing-plus-GPU dashboards are a differentiator to look for.
insights.locator: Azure Managed Prometheus and Grafana scrape
